Proffer

PROF-er · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To proffer offer something to be accepted.

The knight knelt to proffer his sword, hilt-first, as a sign of surrender.

Worked Example

After the long negotiation stalled, the union representative decided to proffer a compromise that neither side had considered.

Formally holding something out, here a compromise, for the other side to accept is exactly what it means to proffer it.

How Proffer Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

offer

offer: present something to be accepted

tender

tender: formally offer or present

Antonyms

withhold

withhold: refuse to give or hand over

retract

retract: take back an offer already made

How Strong Is It? — suggest → proffer → press

suggest vs. proffer

suggest vs. proffer: Suggest is weaker than proffer: to suggest an idea is to float it casually, while to proffer it is a firmer act, formally holding it out to be accepted or refused.

press vs. proffer

press vs. proffer: Press is stronger than proffer: you proffer help and let the other person decide, but to press it on them goes further, insisting so hard it is difficult to refuse.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: forward (Latin)

root — -ffer (ferre)

root — -ffer (ferre): to carry, to bear (Latin, via Old French poroffrir)

Put it together

Put it together: Proffer comes from Old French poroffrir -- pro- ('forward') folded onto offer, itself from Latin ferre, 'to carry.' To proffer something is to carry it forward and hold it out for someone else to take.

Use the root in a new word: transfer

Use the root in a new word: transfer: The bank needed two business days to transfer the funds between the accounts.

Root Check

Word Choice

Proffer is a formal, almost old-fashioned word for offering, and unlike munificent, largesse, or endow elsewhere in this unit, it says nothing about generosity. You can proffer an apology, a resignation, or a tiny tip just as easily as a fortune; the word only describes the act of formally holding something out.
